title: Mindfulness-based nutrition therapy in the treatment of mental illness - nutrition-related competences in a psychiatric context
summary:
Whether it is an appropriate nutrient intake or certain eating styles: the influence of eating habits on mental health has long been discussed in research, with ambivalent results. What is known so far, however, is that mental illnesses can be associated with various nutritional problems such as reduced appetite or a lack of pleasure. Eating often also serves to avoid or regulate unpleasant emotional states. Mindfulness-based approaches are playing an increasingly important role in therapeutic intervention planning as part of the third wave of psychotherapy. 
The effectiveness of mindfulness on mental health has been well researched and scientifically proven. Initial research findings also show positive effects of mindfulness with regard to nutrition, although there are still few data on this. This includes intuitive eating, dealing with cravings or the perception of eating behaviour under the influence of stress. This new study aims to further address this research gap and investigates the effects of multimodal, practice-oriented nutritional therapy on the improvement of nutrition-related skills in the context of mental illness, in addition to conventional research approaches on nutritional-physiological mechanisms of action of nutrition. 
In four modules, each consisting of a theoretical and a practical unit, patients complete a four-week therapy unit in a group therapy setting during partial or full inpatient treatment. They are taught nutrition-specific knowledge with a mindfulness-based focus and prepare meals together independently under therapeutic supervision. The aim is to create a better awareness of one's own diet and the cognitive processes behind it, away from prohibitions and restrictions on food, in order to support long-term recovery. Nutrition and mindfulness-based questionnaires are used to scientifically analyse the influence of a nutritional therapy intervention as part of psychosomatic treatment on eating habits and general psychological stress during and after treatment.
conditions: All patients who are of legal age and capable of giving their consent and who start partial or full inpatient treatment for mental illness at the Wahrendorff Clinic are included. Persons with eating disorders are excluded.

interventions.name: All adult patients in a partial or open inpatient in Wahrendorff Clinic setting who have taken part in the  nutritional therapy programme  ‘Koch | Akademie’ due to existing nutritional diagnoses.
All adult patients in the partial or open inpatient setting of the Wahrendorff Clinic who have not taken part in the ‘Koch | Akademie’ nutritional therapy programme.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All adult patients in partial or full inpatient open treatment at the Wahrendorff Clinic who have a nutritional diagnosis and resulting nutritional problems during admission are recommended for the “Koch | Akademie” nutritional therapy program.  All persons who receive this recommendation and decide to take part in this therapeutic program are included in the intervention group.

All adult patients in partial or full inpatient open treatment at the Wahrendorff Clinic who have no nutritional diagnoses and no resulting nutritional problems during admission are not recommended for the “Koch | Akademie” nutritional therapy program. All persons who do not receive a recommendation are included in the control group.
Exclusion criteria:
Persons who are not able to complete the online questionnaire independently. People who do not have an internet-enabled device or an e-mail address. People who have already taken part in this study to evaluate the “Koch | Akademie” nutritional therapy program. People with eating disorders are excluded from the study.
